title.official: Questioning on affidavit and questioning witnesses

operative_text.controlling:
3.13(1)  The following persons may be questioned by a party
adverse in interest:
(a) a person who makes an affidavit in support of an
originating application;
(b) a person who makes an affidavit in response;
(c) a person who makes an affidavit in reply to a response.
(2)  Subject to rule 3.21, a person may be questioned under oath as
a witness for the purpose of obtaining a transcript of the person’s
evidence for use at the hearing of an originating application.
(3)  A party may question a person whom the party is entitled to
question under this rule by serving on the person an appointment
for questioning.
(4)  Rules 6.16 to 6.20 and 6.38 apply for the purposes of this rule.
(5)  The questioning party must file the transcript of the
questioning.

commentary.text: Rule 3.13 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.13. 1. Scope of Examination (i) Generally It is clear to me that the examination may be as searching and thorough as the party's cross-examination of the witness at the discovery could be. However, it must not extend to matters wholly immaterial or irrelevant to the affidavit. This does not mean to say that the examiner is limited to the four corners of the affidavit but that the questions must be relevant and material to the issues arising from the affidavit. See College Brand Clothes Co. v. Brown 23 Alta. L.R. 363 (C.A.), wherein Harvey C.J.A. said at p. 780: “a cross-examination on an affidavit is for the purpose of testing the truth of the statements in the affidavit”. Also see Alta. Pulpwood Exporting Co. v. Falls Paper & Power Co. (1954), 14 W.W.R. 121 at 125 (Alta. S.C.), where Egbert J. considered the above quote from Harvey C.J.A. and stated: “It seems obvious, therefore, that, for the purpose of testing the truth, the cross-examiner may go further afield in his questions”. There are of course limits to which the questioner can go. In College Brand Clothes Co. v. Brown, Harvey C.J.A. said at p. 783: I do not mean to suggest that there may be no limit to which a plaintiff may carry such examination or require such production. When it sufficiently appears that there is a real defence, depending on questions of fact or involved questions of law, the purpose has been accomplished and the examination should end. It must be kept in mind at all times that the reason for the examination on the affidavit is to assist the court to decide the application, and questions and answers which would not assist the court and would not be relevant to the determination of the issue on the motion nor question the truth of the statement contained in the affidavit or the credibility of the affiant and are obviously questions that should be put on examination for discovery should not be allowed. In J.& H. Singer Invt. Ltd v. Sigma Realty Ltd. (1957), 24 W.W.R. 235 (Alta. C.A.), Johnson J.A. said at p. 238: Turning to the questions which it is sought to have Singer answer, no attempt has been made to show and I am unable to see how any of these questions will assist the court to decide the application before it. They are therefore not relevant to the determination of the issue of the motion. There remains the question of ‘testing the truth of the statement.’ Having regard to the limited nature of the facts deposed to, the question of the truth of the statement contained in the affidavit and the credibility of this witness, if it arises at all, could not be decided by the questions which have been asked, and not answered, in this case. Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 760 Alta. (Q.B.), at 762-63, per Feehan J. In Dy-Reyes v. Carina Holdings Ltd., 2000 ABQB 386, 2000 CarswellAlta 563, 267 A.R. 235, Madam Justice Veit, said, at pp. 246-7: Rule 314(2) establishes that the right to cross-examine on an affidavit “is subject to the same Rules, so far as they are applicable, as the Rules that apply to the examination for discovery of a party”. The scope of that cross-examination has been carefully reviewed by Mason, J., in [Alberta Treasury Branches v. Leahy (1999), 254 A.R. 263 (Q.B.)]: While relevance to the pending motion is the determining factor in setting the scope of cross-examination on an affidavit, the Court also retains discretion in whether a question on cross-examination should be answered. As Master Funduk put it in [Esso Petroleum Canada v. Oyen (Town) (1990), 112 A.R. 10 (Master)]: The same principle [the witness can be cross-examined on anything relevant to the issues at trial] applies to the scope of a cross-examination of an affiant except that ‘issues at trial’ is substituted by ‘issues on motion’. In other words, the scope of a cross-examination of an affiant is defined by the issues on the motion for which the affidavit is tendered. It is not an answer to say that the cross-examiner is going as wide as an examination for discovery. If the motion in question opens everything up, the scope of the cross-examination will indeed be as wide as an examination for discovery. Finally, it must be recalled that Côté, J.A., in [Paszkowski v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration (June 8, 1993), Doc. Edmonton Appeal 9203-0844-A (Alta. C.A.)] stated that it was well settled that cross-examination on an affidavit is limited to the issues in the pending motion for which the affidavit is tendered, and credibility. In Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd. v. Toh, 2000 ABQB 814, 2000 CarswellAlta 1313, 276 A.R. 262, 9 C.P.C. (5th) 350, Madam Justice Johnstone summarized the law as follows: The Court of Appeal in Paszkowski v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1993] A.J. No. 448 (C.A.), stated that it is well settled that cross-examination on an Affidavit is limited to the issues in the pending motion for which the Affidavit is tendered and credibility. However, the Court of Appeal provides no explanation of how far reaching the examination can be in pursuit of the second purpose: assessment of credibility. Subsequently, an extensive review of the law on the scope of cross-examination on an Affidavit was established by Mason, J., in Alberta (Treasury Branches) v. Leahy et al. (1999), 254 A.R. 263 (Q.B.). The principles contained therein can be summarized as follows: • there are key differences between cross-examination on an Affidavit and examinations for discovery: (a) the person examined is a witness not a party; (b) answers given are evidence not admissions; (c) absence of knowledge is an acceptable answer; the witness cannot be required to inform him or herself; (d) production of documents can only be required on the same basis as for any other witness, that is, if the witness has the custody or control of the document; (e) the rules of relevance are more limited; • cross-examination on an Affidavit should not be utilized as a gate into the field of examination for discovery; • cross-examination can be searching, thorough and not bound strictly to the material set out in the four corners of the Affidavit, but is limited to the issues arising from the Affidavit as they relate to the motion to which the Affidavit was filed in support; • questions and answers which would not assist the Court and would not be relevant to the determination of the issue on the motion nor question the truth of the statement contained in the Affidavit or the credibility of the Affiant and are obviously questions that should be put on examination for discovery should not be allowed; • an inquiry into credibility is still limited by the type of application in question; • because the motion judge cannot decide the credibility of Affidavit witnesses (as contrasted with trial witnesses) the scope of cross-examination in respect to credibility would not include cross-examination intended to impeach the character of the witness; however, to the extent that credibility is a relevant issue, all questions may be asked which tend to expose the errors, omissions, inconsistencies, exaggerations or improbabilities of the deponent's testimony contained in his or her Affidavit; such cross-examination is intended to challenge the truth or accuracy of a fact deposed to by removing the foundation for the fact; as such, it is intended to neutralize the probative value of the fact; • while relevance to the pending motion is the determining factor in setting the scope of cross-examination on an Affidavit, the Court also retains a discretion in whether a question on cross-examination should be answered, and may limit questions which are vexatious or irrelevant, excessive or abusive. In International Securities Group Inc. v. Alberta (Securities Commission), 2011 ABQB 737, 2011 CarswellAlta 2315, 530 A.R. 117, Justice Jeffrey commented on the scope of a cross-examination on affidavit. At paragraph 19, Jeffrey, J. said: 19 ISG also refers me to the established law on the scope of examinations not being limited by the scope of the affidavit but by the scope of the issues in the motion for which the affidavit has been tendered, and relies on Fradsham, supra. This is correct, although questioning may also be directed at an affiant's credibility and is subject to the overriding discretion of the Court to determine whether a question should be answered. See, for example, the following cases cited by Fradsham: Paszkowski v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration), [1993] A.J. No. 448, 1993 CarswellAlta 897, [Doc. Edmonton Appeal 9203-0844-A], (Alta. C.A.); Alberta Treasury Branches v. Leahy (1999), 254 A.R. 263 (Q.B.). In relation to questions about seized items, Justice Jeffrey said, at paragraph 27: 27 However, all questioning is permissible that seeks to reveal whether or not the existence or content of a seized item intersects with the nature of the matter (or matters) under investigation, all other things being equal. That wording tracks and adapts to this context the definition of relevance articulated by the Supreme Court of Canada in Deloitte at para.16: “[r]elevance occurs where the nature of the allegations and the content of the disclosed materials intersect.” (ii) When affiant is a non-party The larger issue that has been raised in the context of this application is the scope of the cross examination on the affidavits of non-party affiants who have filed affidavits in opposition to the application. . . . . . … In my view, counsel for the plaintiff is correct in his phrasing of the general proposition, which I understand to be that any question can be asked on the cross examination of an affidavit that is not wholly irrelevant or wholly immaterial that goes to answering the live issues in the litigation… The plaintiff argues, and in my view correctly so, that the scope of cross examination on affidavits in this matter is therefore very broad. Where the difficulty arises however, is whether this same scope should apply to the individuals who have sworn affidavits in this matter who are not parties to the action. The plaintiffs also argue that there is a duty on a deponent to inform him or herself of the matters in issue, and to allow a party to choose a deponent who is not fully informed is unfair, citing the cases of Ethicon Inc. v. Cyanamid of Canada Ltd. (1977), 35 C.P.R. (2d) 126 (Fed. T.D.), and 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1989), 99 A.R. 100 (Master), in support. However, the same difficulty is encountered as both cases deal with affiants who were parties to the litigation. Though the principle as it applies to those affiants is undoubtedly correct, it does not determine the situation here, where the affiants in question are not parties to the litigation. This same criticism can be made of the plaintiff's reliance on the case of Leesona Corp. v. Celanese Canada Ltd. (1974), 14 C.P.R. (2d) 55 (Fed. T.D.), which they correctly cite as standing for the proposition that a cross-examiner on an affidavit is entitled to have produced at the cross examination those documents relevant to the cross examination. The defendant does not take issue with the plaintiff's recitation of the law relating to the scope of a cross examination on an affidavit, they do however argue that this same scope cannot be applied in the case of a non-party affiant. They argue that a non-party affiant is not in the same position as a party, as they have merely agreed to swear an affidavit voluntarily to provide the court with the information in their personal knowledge to aid in the determination of the matter. While they are subject to cross examination on the material in the affidavit that goes to questioning the truth of the statements in the affidavit or are relevant to the credibility of the deponent, they cannot be required to undertake to provide additional information outside of their personal knowledge. The defendant argues that this would simply be an unreasonable onus with which to burden a voluntary affiant. With this statement I agree. It can be imagined that if all affiants were subject to the same burden as parties are for providing information the opposing party feels is relevant to the issue, people not required to swear affidavits (ie. non-parties) may be very hesitant to become involved in the litigation. This, in my view, could result in the court finding itself in the disadvantaged position to make decisions based on a significantly reduced amount of evidence, which could certainly lead to the making of ill-informed decisions. While there does not appear to be any Canadian authority directly on point as to the extent of the examination of non-party affiants, there is some discussion of the issue in the English case of Macmillan Inc. v. Bishopgate Investment Trust Ltd., [1993] 1 W.L.R. 837; affirmed [1993] 4 All E.R. 998 (C.A.). The Court of Appeal held that an order for the production of documents of non-party affiants should not be made unless the court was of the opinion that it was necessary either for disposing fairly of the cause or matter or for saving costs. The court notes that a mere witness cannot be forced by subpoena to produce documents to another party, and such a subpoena would be set aside if likely for discovery purposes only, and the part issuing the subpoena would not enter the documents as evidence at trial… . . . . . I would suggest that this argument can only apply more stringently when the third party affiant does not in fact have power over or possession of the requested documents, and while the reasoning in this case is not binding, it is in my view … the correct approach to take in this situation… … In my view, requiring a non-party affiant to obtain documents that are not within their power or possession, or to undertake to answer questions outside of their personal knowledge, would be unduly oppresive. CRC-Evans Pipeline International Inc. v. O.J. Pipelines Corp. (1996), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 81 (Q.B.), at 82-85, per Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. 2. Cross-examination on Statutory Declaration Exhibited to Affidavit In Alberta Treasury Branches v. Ghermezian (1999), 241 A.R. 107 (Q.B.), an affidavit with a statutory declaration exhibited to it was filed. An application was brought to permit cross-examination of the maker (Leahy) of the statutory declaration. Moore J. concluded that a statutory declaration was included in the term “affidavit” in R. 314(1). However, he dismissed the application, but noted that the court could consider the lack of cross-examination when assessing the weight to be given the evidence. At pp.112-13, His Lordship said: The question then becomes whether Leahy's properly executed “affidavit” triggers the application of rule 314(1). At first blush, the plain wording of rule 314(1) suggests that it does not matter whether the sworn statement is the actual affidavit or an exhibit thereto. It simply provides that a person who has sworn an “affidavit” which is then filed in any action may be cross-examined on that affidavit without order. This would appear to include a solemn declaration filed along with an affidavit. However, the issue here is whether the statutory declaration was filed within the meaning of rule 314(1), simply by being attached as an exhibit. . . . . . Rule 311 provides that any document to be used in conjunction with an affidavit shall be an exhibit to it. I have difficulty with the concept that simply marking a statutory declaration as an exhibit elevates it to the status of an “affidavit” for the purposes of cross-examination. Indeed, rule 312 provides that an exhibit need not even be attached to the affidavit, so long as it is properly marked and brought to court at the time of the application. WEM's choice to attach the statutory declaration for the court's convenience of reference should not subject Leahy to cross-examination. It would be a strange interpretation of the Rules to conclude that a simple choice to attach or not attach a sworn exhibit dictates whether one is required to submit to cross-examination. Further, rule 314(1) itself clearly requires that for a person to be subject to cross-examination, the affidavit must be “filed in an action or proceeding”. In my view, this is an essential point. As WEM noted, an exhibit itself is not “filed in an action or proceeding”, but rather is only a document referred to in an affidavit, which is filed. This is further supported in the treatment of “documents” in rule 8, which provides that the clerk shall file “documents” after an action has been started, that the clerk is to endorse a filing date on “documents” and that the clerk is to make a note on the procedure card that such “documents” have been filed. This is not done with exhibits; rather it is the affidavit that is presented for filing, endorsed with a date and entered on the procedure card. Therefore, I find that although ATB is correct in its position that deponents of filed statutory declarations can be examined pursuant to rule 314(1) as if they had sworn an affidavit, the fact remains that Leahy's statutory declaration has not been filed in accordance with the Rules; it has only been marked as an exhibit to an affidavit which has been filed. Accordingly, I find that Leahy is not required to submit to cross-examination on his statutory declaration. If attaching a sworn statement as an exhibit to an affidavit of another makes the deponent of the exhibit examinable under rule 314(1), it is possible that a witness who never intended to file his statement could be subjected to cross-examination simply by the act of another attaching it to his own affidavit. I am mindful that deponents of sworn statements swear their evidence to be true and therefore should not balk at the possibility of cross-examination; however, fairness dictates that the possibility of being exposed to potential cross-examination due to the acts of another party should be known from the outset. In this case, counsel presented no evidence as to whether Leahy knew of the purpose his statutory declaration would be put [to] by WEM, or even any evidence as to why Leahy made the declaration and how it came to be in WEM's possession. WEM has chosen to put forward statements of Leahy on issues at the very heart of the pending Receivership Application in a form they have successfully argued is not subject at this time to testing by cross-examination. Although rule 305(3) permits this, it is ultimately a matter for the court's discretion and the court may choose to assign little or no weight to the evidence as presented. 3. Duty to Inform If authority is needed that the deponent of an affidavit may be required by order to inform himself about material matters, such may be found in Ethicon Inc. et al. v. Cyanimid Canada Ltd. (1977), 35 C.P.R. (2d) 126 (F.C.T.D.). That case concerned an application to expunge a trademark. A production manager of the respondent had deposed to an affidavit used in opposition to the application. He was cross-examined but was unable to answer some questions put to him. The questions were outside of the four corners of the affidavit but they were material to the application. He was ordered to inform himself and reattend for further cross-examination. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1989), 99 A.R. 100 at 103 (Master). 4. Withdrawal of an Affidavit In R.O.M. Construction Ltd. v. Heeley (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 200 (Q.B.), Justice Veit said, at pp. 205-206: [15] Finally, the court should not permit the withdrawal of an affidavit merely to prevent cross-examination. The solicitor's affidavit was filed and served. One of the earliest statements of the law appears in Clarke v. Law (1855), 69 E.R. 680 at 682: When a party gives notice that he intends to use at the hearing an affidavit made by him, he is both a party and a witness. If he had filed a new affidavit he could not say that he would not use it. He has propounded himself as a witness, and cannot be allowed, if not cross-examined, to use his affidavit, but if threatened with cross-examination to withdraw it: having tendered himself as a witness, he is bound to submit to cross-examination. I have no doubt upon this point… [16] Later in Re Quartz Hill, etc. Co.; ex parte Young (1882), 21 Ch. D. 642 (C.A.), Jessel M.R. states at p. 644: Considering the number of years which have elapsed since Clarke v. Law, [supra] was decided, and considering the good sense of the decision, I should have thought its authority unquestionable had it not been for the observations attributed to Lord Selborne in Pike v. Dickinson, 21 W.R. 862, which probably are incorrectly reported, and which I do not understand. The principle of Clarke v. Law is quite intelligible—a party who has given notice to read an affidavit is not entitled to withdraw it in order to avoid cross-examination. He need not use the evidence if he does not like it. So a party who has called a witness is not to withdraw him in order to avoid his being cross-examined. This is good sense, and in my opinion, we are not now at liberty to decline to follow that decision. [17] Brett L.J. states at pp. 645-46: As regards the principle laid down by Lord Hatherley in Clarke v. Law I consider it a principle applicable not merely to a proceeding in Chancery or at Common Law, but to proceedings before every tribunal. Every rule of procedure ought to be framed with a view to its being such that if it be properly acted upon the course of justice will be kept pure and undefiled. With this view I think it most important that no person who has taken a step with a view to gaining an advantage should be at liberty to withdraw it if he finds that it will not answer. Lord Hatherley accordingly held that where a party had proposed himself as a witness and filed an affidavit, he could not, when threatened with cross-examination, withdraw the affidavit and escape cross-examination. I cannot imagine anything more calculated to bring the course of justice into contempt than to allow a person to file evidence which if there is no cross-examination makes in his favour, but which he knows will break down on cross-examination, and then to withdraw it if he finds that cross-examination is threatened. [18] Cotton L.J. states at p. 646: I am not satisfied that the Act, independently of any authority does not by its plain terms prevent the witness being withdrawn, for it makes a person liable to attend to be cross-examined who has made and filed an affidavit to be used or which shall be used. Be this as it may, the rule was laid down in Clarke v. Law in 1855, that a person who has made an affidavit cannot be withdrawn from cross-examination. It is a good rule, and one which ought to be followed. The question has been raised whether the decision applies to a person not a party to the cause or matter, but Lord Hatherley appears to lay down the rule generally, and it has been acted upon in practice. Whatever, therefore, the true construction of the Act may be, I think it is now too late to take a different view from that which has been so long acted on. [19] Later yet, Lord Denning in Comet Products U.K. Ltd. v. Hawkex Plastics Ltd., [1971] 2 W.L.R. 361 (C.A.), commented on Clarke v. Law and Re Quartz Hill, etc. Co.; ex parte Young at p. 366 by saying: Those cases show that in ordinary civil proceedings in Chancery, if an affidavit is filed and used before the court, the defendant, when he is threatened with cross-examination, cannot get out of it by saying that he will withdraw his affidavit. If he has filed an affidavit, and in addition has gone on to use it in the court, then he is liable to be cross-examined upon it if the court thinks it right so to order. I would not say that the mere filing is sufficient, but I do say that when it is not only filed but used, the defendant does expose himself to a liability to be cross-examined if the judge so rules. (i) Right to cross-examine In R.O.M. Construction Ltd. v. Heeley (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 200 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Veit, though dealing with the previous Rules [R. 314(1)], said: [13] Rule 314(1) states that a person who has made an affidavit filed in any action or proceedings may be cross-examined on the affidavit without order. Such an examination, given as of right in the Rules, should be denied only in unusual circumstances. No such circumstances have been alleged [in this case]. The court should not impose its judgment on that of the opposite party as to whether an examination would be valuable or would necessarily advance the positions of the party opposite. [Emphasis added.] In Canada (Attorney General) v. Sandford (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 170 (Q.B.), at 174, Justice Miller said: The operative word in s. 314(1) [sic] is “may” and there are some decisions from the Supreme Court of Canada construing the use of the word “may” in the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act which confer a discretion upon the court to allow or disallow an action or a step in an action. See R. v. Potvin (1989), 47 C.C.C. (3d) 289 at 304–306; R. v. Corbett (1988), 41 C.C.C. (3d) 385 at 428-29 … I can foresee some extreme sets of facts which would still give a court the discretion to refuse the right to cross-examine on an affidavit but I accept the proposition that this discretion should be exercised sparingly and only in clearest of situations. In the case at bar I am not prepared to hold, at this stage of the proceedings, that the defendant's requested examination on the affidavit is totally frivolous or designed only to stall the resolution of the matter. In Reference re Firearms Act (Canada) (1998), 228 A.R. 35 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal, at paragraph 8, quoted with approval Veit J.'s statement in R.O.M. Construction Ltd. v. Heeley (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 200 (Q.B.), that “Rule 314(1) states that a person who has made an affidavit filed in any action or proceeding may be cross-examined on the affidavit without order. Such an examination, given as a right in the Rules, should be denied only in unusual circumstances.” The Court of Appeal said, at p. 38: Although the rule requiring cross-examination may not be absolute, it does provide that a party is entitled to cross-examination “as of course”… No unusual circumstances exist in this Reference sufficient to deny Alberta the opportunity to cross-examine Professor Killias on his affidavit. The Court of Appeal in Becker v. Alberta (Director of Employment Standards), 2000 ABCA 329, 2000 CarswellAlta 1539, 277 A.R. 131, 7 C.P.C. (5th) 41, commented on Veit J.'s decision in R.O.M. Construction Ltd. v. Heeley (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 200 in the course of deciding that a Chambers judge had not erred in denying the appellant an adjournment in order to cross-examine on the affidavit filed in support of a summary judgment application brought against the appellant. At p. 137, the court said: Counsel for Becker conceded that denial of an adjournment for the purpose of cross-examination is discretionary, but submitted that where the affidavits are in support of a summary judgment, an adjournment to cross-examine is virtually automatic and should only be denied in special circumstances. He relied on the judgment of Veit, J., in R.O.M. Construction Ltd. v. Heeley et al. … The statement of Veit, J., does not apply in this case where the summary judgment was granted on the basis that the action was barred because of the expiry of the limitation period. Here, there was no position of Becker to advance by evidence on the limitation issue. No further evidence relevant to the limitation issue could be gained from cross-examining the respondents' affiants. The evidence as to when Becker received the decision of the Umpire was within Becker's knowledge, not the respondents'. The computation of the limitation period is a matter of law, not facts. The time of filing the originating notice was apparent on the face of the record. The one matter which the appellant could have examined on was the time of service of his originating notice on the respondents. However, as discussed above, this fact was not necessary to determine the limitations issue in light of the late filing of the originating notice. In Point on the Bow Development Ltd. v. William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd. (2004), 25 Alta. L.R. (4th) 220 (C.A.), the Court reviewed when one would not be permitted to cross-examine on an affidavit. At p. 174, the Court said: The appellant's particular complaint is the case management judge's refusal to grant an adjournment to permit cross-examination on the affidavit filed in support of the respondent's contempt motion. Although R. 314(1) provides that any person who makes an affidavit may be cross-examined without order, the right to cross-examine is not absolute or unlimited: Bank of Montreal v. Lysyk 2003 ABQB 47, even in relation to a contempt application: Continuing Care Employers' Bargaining Assn. v. Alberta Union of Public Employees (2002), 303 A.R. 137, 273 W.A.C. 137, 2002 ABCA 148. A request to cross-examine may be denied in instances where the examination would be totally frivolous or is only designed to forestall the proceedings: Canada (Attorney General) v. Sandford (1995), 175 A.R. 118 (Q.B.), at para. 17 (Q.B.). While certain facts may exist that would give a court the discretion to refuse the right to cross-examine on an affidavit, “this discretion should be exercised sparingly and only in clearest of situations”: Sandford, id. See also Reference Re Firearms Act (Can.) (1998), 228 A.R. 35, 188 W.A.C. 35, 1998 ABCA 306. In Fech v. Lewington, 2022 ABCA 154, the Court said again that a party “‘has an almost absolute right to cross-examine on an affidavit, at to get an adjournment for that if he or she seeks it properly, even if the affidavit is unnecessary or irrelevant, or the party filing it seeks to withdraw it’: Stevenson & Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1999) at 226.” (ii) Effect of inability to cross-examine In Reference re Firearms Act (Canada) (1998), 228 A.R. 35 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal of an order of Côté J.A. (as a case manager) in which he held that an inability to cross-examine on an affidavit constituted grounds to rule that the affidavit was inadmissible. At pp. 37-38 of the Court of Appeal decision, Côté J.A.'s comments were reproduced. Côté J.A. said: One might think that cross-examination or the right to cross-examine only goes to weight, and not to admissibility. By one of life's strange coincidences, I was looking up the law of cross-examination for a different case this morning and stumbled across a passage in Halsbury's Laws (v. 15, p.443 n. (c), 3d ed.) which says that inability to cross-examine is a ground to exclude evidence; the case cited is Allen v. Allen, [1894] P. 248 (C.A.) @ pp. 253-54, a decision of the English Court of Appeal which supports that view. That was a case where the trial judge denied a certain party the right to cross-examine a witness called by a party on the same side as the one who wished to cross-examine. The Court of Appeal held that the denial had been improper, and that that rendered the evidence inadmissible. In Hoda v. Hoda, 2021 ABCA 122, 2021 CarswellAlta 783, Justice Slatter said (at paragraph 5): [5]… The general rule is that if the affiant refuses to be cross-examined, the affidavit is not admitted or given no weight: Reference re: Firearms Act (Can), 1998 ABCA 306, 86 Alta LR (3d) 59; R. v Darrach, 2000 SCC 46 at paras. 61-62, [2000] 2 SCR 443. No one is allowed to put one-sided, unchallenged evidence on the record. … (iii) Filing one's own affidavit not required One is not required to file an affidavit before cross-examining on the opponent's affidavit. In my opinion this rule gives an interested party the right to cross-examine on an affidavit which has been filed in the action. That right is not qualified in any way. It would be a derogation from the right given by the rule for me to attach conditions to the cross-examination. The defendant may obtain sufficient qualification or admissions from the plaintiff on the cross-examination that the defendant is certain it will be successful in opposing the plaintiff's summary judgment application without filing its own affidavit. Defendants sometimes make that decision to their own regret, but it is their own decision to make. The plaintiff may suggest that it is somehow unfair for the plaintiff to be exposed to cross-examination before the defendant is required to put in any affidavit at all. The plaintiff has the onus of proving its case, and if its case is a proper one for summary judgment it should not fear any affidavit that can be filed by the defendant, even after the defendant has had the opportunity of both reading and cross-examination on the plaintiff's affidavit. At a trial the plaintiff puts in his evidence first and is subject to cross-examination before the defendant is required to lead any of his evidence. I would accordingly order that the plaintiff's application be adjourned for three weeks from the date of these reasons to allow the defendant to cross-examine on the affidavit of the plaintiff. The said adjournment is not conditional upon the defendant filing an affidavit in opposition to the plaintiff's affidavit. Bullex Developments Ltd. v. Terra Mines Ltd. (1984), 31 Alta. L.R. (2d) 93 at 94 (Master). 5. Loss of Right to Cross-examine Due to Delay It is true that a right to cross-examine may be lost by delay, especially where that would mean delaying the hearing of the motion … Maybe delaying cross-examination long enough might itself remove the right to cross-examine. But 3 or 4-months delay which does not delay the motion, and does not result in prejudice, cannot do that. Armstrong v. Esso Resources Canada Ltd. (1992), 10 C.P.C. (3d) 343 Alta. (C.A.), at 344, per Côté J.A. 6. Failure to File Undertakings Counsel for the defendant has not provided me with the responses to the undertakings. The assumption I make from that is that the responses would not weaken the plaintiff's case in any manner or, conversely, show a triable issue about interest. Alberta Treasury Branches v. Acorn (1987), 83 A.R. 215 (Master), at 230, per Master Funduk. And in another decision Master Funduk stated: There were four undertakings given on the cross-examination. Counsel made no reference to them in their submissions, and did not provide me with any answers to the undertakings. If the undertakings were not complied with I conclude counsel for the applicant defendants has waived compliance with the undertakings. If the undertakings were complied with I conclude that the responses were not favourable to the applicant defendants, and were favourable to the plaintiff. It was the responsibility of counsel for the applicant defendants to provide me with copies of the responses to the undertakings if responses were given. McGinn (Gerald) Drilling Ltd. v. Hampton Securities Ltd. (1985), 64 A.R. 93 at 94 (Master).

BOOK_C.title: Questioning on affidavit and questioning witnesses
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 2 – ACTIONS STARTED BY ORIGINATING APPLICATION

commentary.text:
These rules set out the permissible questioning that can take place in relation to an affidavit filed in an originating application. The questioning is not discovery, but is in the nature of a cross-examination and the transcript must be filed (rule 6.20(5)(b)).
Nature of the Cross Examination – When questioning on an affidavit in support of an application, questions relevant to the underlying application are permitted, and if they are refused, the court may order that they be answered. “[I]ssues relevant to the application are not confined to the ‘four corners of the affidavit’. . . . Cross-examination may be ‘searching, thorough and not bound strictly to the material set out in . . . the Affidavit, but is limited to issues arising from the Affidavit as they relate to the motion’. . . . In order to determine what information or documents are relevant . . ., the Court must review the issues in the underlying Originating Application.”. Real Estate Council of Alberta v. Moser, [2019] A.J. No. 222, 2019 ABQB 106 at paras. 11-14 (Alta. Q.B.), citing , [2000] A.J. No. 1345, 2000 ABQB Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd. v. Toh Adversity in Interest – Adversity in interest is a flexible concept. It must be determined by examining the pleadings and the factual context of the case. Precision Drilling Canada Ltd. v. Yangarra Resources Ltd., [2013] A.J. No. 976, 2013 ABQB 492 at para. 53 (Alta. Q.B.), citing , [1996] A.J. Trizec Equities Ltd. v. Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd. No. 699, 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 442 at para. 15 (Alta. Q.B.).
Credibility – During questioning, a deponent’s credibility can be called into question; this is subject to the overriding discretion of the court to determine whether a question should be
